newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cohen visit to Japan assures future for US troops.
newsitem.headline: Cohen visit to Japan assures future for US troops.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen ended a visit to Japan on Wednesday which confirmed a continued American military presence in Asia no matter what happens in China and North Korea.

Making his first trip to Asia since becoming defence secretary, Cohen sent a strong signal that there would be no troop cutbacks into the 21st century and the American military presence was the best guarantee of peace in the region.
His message was strongly backed by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto who told Cohen he could rely on Tokyo remaining the United States' chief ally in Asia.

During the three day visit, Cohen also lectured U.S. forces on the need to act as "ambassadors", "diplomats", "emissaries" if they wanted to be welcome in the fast-growing area which has become crucial to the United States' own economic future.
Cohen argued that a reduction of American troop numbers in the western Pacific could trigger an arms race in Asia.

"If we were to have a substantial reduction of our force in the region, I believe that would set up a very negative dynamic, namely other countries would then feel an obligation to start arming themselves to a much higher level than they currently are," he told reporters on Tuesday.
"That would not bode well for the region. It might, in fact, contribute to greater potential for conflict, which is something we do not want."
Cohen repeatedly stated that the 100,000 U.S. troops in Asia, most of them in Japan and South Korea, were there to stay and were not aimed at containing the growing military might of China.
"It is not designed against China at all, but to maintain stability in the region," Cohen said.
This was welcome news for Japanese officials who worry that a more expansionist China could challenge their economic influence through the region.
But Cohen's forthright comment that even if North and South Korea unified, American troops would remain in South Korea in the same numbers caused a slight ripple during his visit.
Cohen said he did not believe troop levels in South Korea should be reduced over the short term, even if peace were to come to the peninsula.
He said the situation in heavily armed North Korea was very unstable.

Japanese policy makers use the possibility of a threat from communist North Korea as one of their main arguments in a battle with the southern island of Okinawa about the future of U.S. military bases there.
Okinawa, an island that makes up less than one percent of Japan's land area, hosts 75 percent of the U.S. bases in Japan.
In a non-binding referendum last year, Okinawans backed a drive by the island's governor to close all bases by 2015.
In a final meeting between Cohen and Hashimoto on Wednesday, they pledged to try to cut the burden on the island but gave no ground in saying the number of troops would remain the same.
"It was a very good exchange. There was a commitment on the part of the prime minister to maintain the U.S. presence (in the Pacific)," Cohen said while en route from Japan to Seoul, South Korea.
He said that any change in the number of troops would be done in consultation with Japan.
